title: The Rigveda — the Samhita text in Sanskrit
attributionNote: The hymns were composed by many priestly families over centuries and are attributed within the text to named seers, one family of seers to each hymn. No single author is claimed for the collection, and the tradition of the seer of each hymn is carried in the index rather than asserted here.
description: The Rigveda is the oldest of the Vedas and the oldest religious poetry in an Indo-European language: 1,028 hymns to Agni the fire, Indra the thunderer, Soma the drink of the sacrifice, Varuna the guardian of the oath, Ushas the dawn and the other powers, with the hymns of creation and of the cosmic order in the tenth book. The text here is the Samhita — the continuous collection of the hymns as they were recited, without the priestly prose of the Brahmanas or the rules of the Vedangas.
historicalContext: The hymns were composed in the northwest of the subcontinent and were fixed as a canonical collection with the accent and the word-by-word recitation preserved. The Aufrecht edition of 1877 is the standard grapheme-level text still cited by Vedic scholars, and the digital form used here is the one prepared by Van Nooten and Holland, checked against it rather than copied from a single printed page.
availabilityNote: Complete: the ten mandalas and 1,028 hymns of the Samhita in the Aufrecht edition, streamed from GRETIL at read time one hymn at a time. This is the Sanskrit original; the English verse translation the library already holds (Griffith, 1896) is a separate record.
